items.q: Why write a short spec before asking the AI to build?
options: It is required before any code will run
It makes the AI generate code more quickly
Specs are only needed by big companies and legal teams
The AI builds fast, so if you haven't decided what you want it will build the wrong thing fast — the spec makes you decide first

explain.right: Deciding what you actually want is the hard part; a short spec settles that up front and saves hours of 'no, not like that'.
explain.wrong: Specs help solo beginners most, they don't speed up or gate code execution — their value is deciding intent before building.

items.q: Which of these is a good acceptance criterion for a habit tracker?
options: It should be fast and reliable
The app should look nice and modern
A user can add a habit and it appears in the list

explain.right: It describes observable user behavior you can test yes/no: do the action, check the result.
explain.wrong: 'Nice', 'latest framework', and 'fast/reliable' aren't checkable — they're vague wishes or tech choices, not pass/fail tests.

items.q: What is the point of acceptance criteria?
options: A list of the technologies you'll use
A design mockup of the screens
A marketing description of the app
Concrete, checkable statements of 'it works' that tell you (and the AI) when a feature is done

explain.right: They turn a fuzzy goal into yes/no tests of user-visible behavior, so you know when to stop building a feature.
explain.wrong: Tech lists, mockups, and marketing copy aren't pass/fail checks of whether the thing actually works.

items.q: Your first-build spec has grown to 20 features. What's the best move?
options: Build all 20 at once — the AI is fast enough
Cut it down to a small core you can actually finish; keeping scope small is a feature
Add a few more so it's complete
Skip the spec and just start coding

explain.right: A small thing you finish beats a big thing you abandon; guarding scope is a deliberate strength, not a weakness.
explain.wrong: Piling on features (or dropping the spec) is how first builds stall — trim to a finishable core instead.

items.q: Write one acceptance criterion for an app that lets you save short notes.
rubric: Describes observable, user-visible behavior (an action and its result)
Is checkable yes/no (you could perform it and see pass/fail)
Ties to the app's purpose (saving/seeing a note), e.g. 'I can type a note, save it, and it still shows after I refresh'

explain.right: Strong answers state an action plus the expected visible result you can test, like 'I can save a note and it reappears after refresh'.
explain.wrong: A weak answer is a vague wish like 'notes should be good' with nothing to check.
